articles.title: 4 takeaways from Braves' sweep of Dodgers include Atlanta's Chris Sale flexing and L.A.'s continued tinkering of rotation
articles.summary: While there's real comfort in having snagged the tiebreaker over the Dodgers this week, the Braves still have plenty of more work to do to avoid having to pl...
articles.body:
Until Atlanta's uncharacteristic down season in 2025, the Braves and Dodgers enjoyed a lengthy parallel run as the gold standards atop the National League. From 2018-2024, they racked up more regular-season wins than any other NL team by a healthy margin and made annual trips to the postseason. During that run, they met three times in October. The Dodgers toppled the Braves in the 2018 NLDS en route to the pennant. In 2020, L.A. again emerged victorious over Atlanta in the NLCS in seven games on their path to claiming the franchise's first title since 1988. The Braves returned the favor a year later, eliminating the Dodgers in the NLCS on their own march to a long-awaited World Series title.

Since then, however, clashes between the two powerhouses have been limited to the regular season. That could change this year. Atlanta's resurgence has restored a familiar picture atop the National League standings, with both the Braves and Dodgers jockeying with the Brewers for the top overall seed and the two byes surpassing the wild-card round. A potential preview of another epic postseason showdown unfolded this week at Truist Park, with the Braves sweeping the Dodgers , winning all three games by one run apiece. Right-hander Bryce Elder turned in a quality start before Ozzie Albies drove in the go-ahead run in the eighth inning as Atlanta took the series opener 4-3. Another back-and-forth nailbiter ensued Wednesday that also fell in the Braves' favor, this time in walk-off fashion, 6-5. The series concluded Thursday with a gem of a pitchers' duel between Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Sale stole the show by throwing a spectacular complete game shutout to preserve a 1-0 victory — with the lone run coming on Drake Baldwin's solo homer on Yamamoto's first pitch of the game — and nail down the sweep for the Braves.

Here are four takeaways from this week's marquee matchup in Atlanta:

If you needed any additional evidence that this week's series had a little extra juice, look no further than 37-year-old Chris Sale unleashing his hardest recorded pitch in more than eight years : a 100.1-mph heater to Shohei Ohtani in the top of the third inning that Ohtani fouled off before succumbing to Sale's signature slider a couple pitches later.

Two innings later, Sale again brought some bonus heat against Ohtani, this time 99.6 mph — also harder than any other pitch he had thrown as a Brave before Thursday — that blazed past Ohtani's vicious hack above the zone for his second strikeout of the night. These were just two of Sale's 11 punchouts in the outing, a complete-game masterclass on 109 pitches that featured five hits and zero walks. It was Sale's first complete game since June 5, 2019.

Watching Sale rise to the occasion Thursday to help Atlanta complete the sweep, outpitching another ace in Yamamoto along the way, evoked an aura of October that was difficult to deny. But that postseason-like buzz Sale and the Braves built in front of nearly 40,000 fans at Truist Park was also a reminder of a strange reality: Sale has still yet to start a playoff game as a Brave, and hasn't appeared in any October contest since the 2021 ALCS with Boston. Severe back spasms rendered Sale unavailable for Atlanta's brief postseason run in 2024, a sour finish to his incredible debut season with the Braves that earned him his first career Cy Young Award. And though Sale finished strong and healthy in 2025, the Braves failed to qualify for the postseason for the first time since 2017.

Now here we are, fresh off an electric reminder of what Sale looks like at his best in a high-stakes ballgame, a little more than a month away from the future Hall-of-Famer's long-awaited return to the postseason stage, barring another freak injury scare a la 2024. Sale already has one World Series title on his résumé having recorded the final out for Boston in 2018 against — you guessed it — the Dodgers. But after what happened two years ago, you can be sure Sale is plenty motivated to maintain his dominance and durability from now until deep into October. And with so many question marks remaining for the rest of Atlanta's rotation, Sale's outings will be especially pivotal for Atlanta's chances of making a real run at a championship.

Few units have shape-shifted more frequently over the past few years than the Dodgers' rotation, which has shuffled through an astonishing range of impact arms and innings eaters in their quest to cover the marathon that is the regular season before the real stuff starts in October. This week brought another wave of arrivals and departures to L.A.'s starting staff, some planned, some unexpected. It began Tuesday with the return of right-hander Tyler Glasnow, making his first start with the Dodgers since May 6 after being sidelined with a back injury. After surrendering three runs in the first inning on a series of bloop hits, Glasnow settled in to complete five frames with seven strikeouts and only that initial trio of runs allowed. His fastball climbed to 97.4 mph and he leaned more on his slider (26%) than his more typical go-to breaking ball, the knuckle-curve (13%), but generally looked like the Glasnow we know.

Wednesday was mercurial right-hander Roki Sasaki's turn to take the mound, but the 24-year-old lasted only 3 1/3 innings before being removed due to a blister on his right middle-finger , which was apparently serious enough to necessitate placing him on the injured list Thursday. For all his confounding ups and downs, Sasaki has been admirably available throughout this season, taking the ball every turn through the rotation, something only Yamamoto can say among all other Dodgers hurlers. But even as Sasaki began to finally find his footing as a more reliable starter, he was unlikely to crack the Dodgers' projected postseason rotation with the names ahead of him on the depth chart. Now he'll be sidelined for an indeterminate amount of time, adding a layer of uncertainty to his role in October and the challenge of returning from injury (even a minor one) as the stakes are climbing. For now, veteran lefty Eric Lauer — who has quietly covered 69 innings to the tune of a 3.78 ERA for Los Angeles this season after being traded by Toronto in mid-May — is expected to step into Sasaki's spot in the rotation.

More movement awaits this weekend in Detroit, and that doesn't even include the highly anticipated homecoming of Tarik Skubal , who is slated to face his former team at Comerica Park on Friday. The other biggest news nugget from the week in Atlanta involved an update on Shohei Ohtani, who last pitched on July 3 but has since paused his mound responsibilities while battling left knee and right bicep discomfort. Manager Dave Roberts said Ohtani will throw a bullpen Friday in Detroit with the possibility of returning to the rotation — at least in an abbreviated role — as soon as Sunday. Glasnow is still expected to pitch Sunday in some form, whether that be following an inning of Ohtani or as a full start with Ohtani instead returning Tuesday at home against St. Louis. Regardless, Ohtani is expected to slowly build his workload back up over the final month of the regular season with the goal of him being prepared to make full-length starts again come October. How many innings Ohtani racks up down the stretch will have a big impact on not only his readiness for the postseason, but also possibly his chances of snatching the NL MVP back from the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong. This weekend is a crucial first step.

Braves' shortstop odyssey: Is this the positive turning point for Ha-Seong Kim?

Ever since Dansby Swanson departed in free agency following the 2022 season, the shortstop position has been one of the stranger subplots for the Braves. Orlando Arcia, Swanson's first replacement, emerged as an unlikely All-Star in 2023 but ended up as a punch line in October thanks to Bryce Harper and then cratered offensively in 2024, loosening his grip on the starting job. Nick Allen followed in 2025 and brought sparkling defense but next-to-nothing with the bat, making his role as the starter untenable. Allen was then traded to Houston for Mauricio Dubón, who has handled shortstop admirably this year but is still better suited for a superutility role. All together, a whopping 17 different players have suited up at shortstop for Atlanta since Swanson left, including 10 over the past two seasons alone — more than any other team in MLB — and those players have combined to produce 3.3 fWAR and a 73 wRC+ at the position, both marks ranking last in the league .

The latest twist in the Braves' ongoing shortstop saga came Wednesday night. With rookie Jim Jarvis sent down to Triple-A earlier in the week, Dubón resumed his role as the starting shortstop. But a series of managerial maneuverings resulted in Atlanta forfeiting the DH and in need of a pinch-hitter in the bottom of the ninth when the pitcher's spot came up with two outs and the winning run on second base. That prompted manager Walt Weiss to turn to Ha-Seong Kim off the bench, despite Kim having contributed virtually nothing this season due to a combination of injuries and woeful underperformance. He stepped to the plate against Dodgers closer Tanner Scott 0 for his last 30 at-bats, having not recorded a hit since June 3 and having collected only five hits all season. Sure enough, Kim smoked a full-count fastball from Scott up the middle for a walk-off single against all odds and his signature moment as a Brave — not that there were many other candidates.

Kim arrived in Atlanta almost exactly a year ago when the Braves claimed him off waivers following a failed abbreviated stint with the Rays after signing as a free agent. The idea was to buy low on the historically steady Kim as a possible everyday shortstop solution, but Kim held a $16 million player option for 2026 that he declined after the season. Then Atlanta re-asserted its interest in Kim by re-signing him to a one-year, $20 million deal, but Kim tore a ligament in his finger slipping on ice in his native South Korea in January, delaying the start to his season until mid-May. An aggravation of that same finger then cost him all of July, turning his first full season as a Brave into an afterthought. Until Wednesday, of course.

As a reward for his walk-off, Kim got the start at shortstop in Thursday's series finale and collected one of Atlanta's four hits against Yoshinobu Yamamoto while striking out in his other plate appearance. After such a miserable and unproductive stint to this point, it would be astounding to see Kim reclaim his post at shortstop moving forward, but his stunning resurgence this week sure has added a layer of intrigue to the rest of his season, especially at such a vital position for a contending team like Atlanta.

Having already won two of three at Dodger Stadium in early May, the Braves' sweep this week in Atlanta secured a highly valuable tiebreaker over the Dodgers. That means that if the Dodgers and Braves finish with the same record (and the second-best record in the league behind, presumably, Milwaukee), it will be Atlanta that automatically advances to the Division Series and await its opponent while the Dodgers would be subjected to the best-of-three wild-card series for the second straight year. That said, the Dodgers still have a better overall record for now at 80-54, a game ahead of the Braves, and L.A. has a notably less daunting strength of schedule the rest of the way. In fact, no National League team has a less challenging remaining slate than the Dodgers, whose only series left against teams that currently have winning records are a trip to Miami and a three-game set at home against the Padres in the final week of the season.

Meanwhile, Atlanta still has seven games left against the division rival Phillies, plus three games at home against AL leader Tampa Bay, and trips to the Cubs, Astros and Marlins. All those games left against Philadelphia will force the Braves to focus on defending their divisional lead before worrying about chasing down the Dodgers. The Brewers, while maintaining a larger cushion, face a similar dynamic with seven more games against the rival Cubs, but the rest of their September slate is a fair bit softer, so their chances of nailing down the top seed are still looking good.

All of which is to say: While there's real comfort in having snagged the tiebreaker over the Dodgers this week, the Braves still have plenty of more work to do to avoid having to play in that nerve-wracking opening round.

articles.title: After 111 Years, George Lombard Jr. on Wrong Side of Yankees History with Rare Stat Recorded
articles.summary: New York Yankees rookie George Lombard Jr. finds himself on the wrong side of history amid his ongoing defensive struggles at shortstop.
articles.body:
New York Yankees rookie George Lombard Jr. finds himself on the wrong side of history amid his ongoing defensive struggles at shortstop.

After a defensive miscue in the eighth inning of Thursday's 5-1 loss to the Houston Astros, Lombard became the first Yankees shortstop since Roger Peckinpaugh in 1915 to commit at least one error in six consecutive games.

Speaking to reporters after Thursday's loss, Lombard talked about his "not acceptable" defensive play:

"It's something we're trying to figure out. It's not acceptable. It can't happen at this level. If you make your pitchers have to get extra outs it just makes it way harder on us, and teams are going to capitalize. So it's something that we're definitely going to have to clean up and I've got to be better tomorrow."

Lombard, who has a total of seven errors in 20 games since being called up, began his current streak against the Toronto Blue Jays on Aug. 21. He has six errors in 29 total chances during this stretch.

For comparison, Arizona Diamondbacks shortstop Geraldo Perdomo has six errors in 516 chances this season.

This is very uncharacteristic for Lombard because scouting reports often touted his defensive ability as arguably his best tool. He's still very young, having turned 21 on June 2, so this rough patch isn't a referendum on his entire career.

It is, however, something Yankees manager Aaron Boone needs to be mindful of given that they are trying to catch the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. They are also only two games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the No. 1 wild card spot with those two teams set to begin a four-game series in the Bronx on Friday night.

articles.title: Chris Sale Reacts to Complete-Game Shutout vs. Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers After Braves Win
articles.summary: Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale reacted to his complete-game shoutout during the team's 1-0 victory over Shohei Ohtani and the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night.
articles.body:
Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale reacted to his complete-game shoutout during the team's 1-0 victory over Shohei Ohtani and the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night.

"I wish I could tell you I knew it was gonna be like that," Sale said during a Friday appearance on the Pat McAfee Show (0:57 mark). "Anytime you're facing a team like that, you just try to put your best foot forward. You know it's gonna be a dogfight, you know it's not gonna come easy."

The 37-year-old tossed 109 pitches in nine innings against the Dodgers, amassing 11 strikeouts without giving up a walk. Sale allowed just five hits as well.

The veteran also discussed the example that he wants to set for the next generation of players.

"I'm doing things that I learned from the guys before me," Sale said Friday (1:51 mark). "I hope if there's something that I do or something that I say or a way I do something, it resonates with somebody and they can use it and then they pass it on. That's a cool thing."

The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has been in the conversation for the honor this year.

Sale is in the midst of a dominant 2026 campaign, owning a 13-9 record in 24 starts to go along with a 2.06 ERA and 1.000 WHIP. He's averaging 11.1 strikeouts compared to a mere 1.8 walks per nine innings.

The Braves currently sit atop the NL East standings with a 79-55 record.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal gets emotional during highly anticipated return to Detroit after blockbuster trade
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal got misty-eyed during a tribute video and standing ovation at Comerica Park before facing former teammate Gleyber Torres on the mound.
articles.body: Earlier this month, the Los Angeles Dodgers pulled off a blockbuster trade with the Detroit Tigers that brought aboard two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. Now, just weeks later, the Dodgers rolled into Motor City, and guess who got the start? … Yes, Tarik Skubal. TARIK SKUBAL SAYS HE WAS EMOTIONAL LEAVING DETROIT TIGERS FOR LA DODGERS, WOULD LOVE TO RETURN: 'I'M CRYING' Outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handed pitchers Brady Smith and River Ryan went the other way in the deal. Skubal's return to Detroit came at an interesting time as the NL West leaders came into the evening fresh off of three-straight losses to the Atlanta Braves. So, despite all of the emotions, Skubal had some important work to do on the hill. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Those emotions briefly got the best of him when the Tigers played a tribute video on the big screen. The right-hander got a little misty-eyed as fans gave him a standing ovation. Detroit's Drew Anderson went through the first half-inning with a pair of strikeouts early, and with that it was time for Skubal to take the mound at Comerica Park in a Dodgers uniform. A mix of boos and cheers as he walked out onto the field. However, before he threw his first pitch, there was a light-hearted moment when Skubal's PitchCom wasn't working right. The Tigers' second baseman, Gleyber Torres, was the first former teammate Skubal had to face, and it didn't go particularly well as he sent a pitch deep to center field over Dodger Alek Thomas' head for a double. articles.title: Tarik Skubal's Box Score Player Stats, Highlights from Dodgers-Tigers in Revenge Game After Trade
articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal struck out seven batters after making an emotional return to his former city.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal struck out seven batters after making an emotional return to his former city.

Skubal pitched six innings Friday in his first outing against the Detroit Tigers since his Aug. 2 trade to the Dodgers.

Here's a look at how Skubal did in his first game as a visiting player at Comerica Park.

The Tigers welcomed Skubal back to Detroit by sharing a tribute video celebrating his six and a half seasons in the city.

Skubal allowed a leadoff double from Gleyber Torres on his second pitch of the game.

He bounced back by forcing Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle into consecutive strikeouts before closing out a scoreless first inning.

Skubal built on that momentum by retiring the next nine batters he faced, including striking out the side in the third frame.

Skubal ran into trouble in the bottom of the fifth after he allowed a leadoff double from Eduardo Valencia.

He was within one strike of closing out the inning when Max Clark connected with his fastball to score an RBI triple.

Skubal gave up another leadoff hit in the bottom of the sixth but got his last three outs in quick succession to close out the no-decision.

He finished the outing having thrown 56 strikes on 83 pitches as the game headed into the seventh in a 1-1 tie.

Since the trade the Dodgers have been leaning heavily on Skubal, who threw more than 100 pitches in each of his prior two starts.

The Dodgers could be hoping this heavy usage will help Skubal adjust to his new club before helping the franchise attempt a World Series three-peat this fall.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal wipes away tears in return to Detroit, then throws 6 strong innings for Dodgers
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal returned to Comerica Park 26 days after the biggest move of the MLB trade deadline.
articles.body:
The biggest deal of the 2026 MLB trade deadline came full circle Friday, with Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal returning to his previous home of Comerica Park.

The Detroit Tigers welcomed the two-time Cy Young Award winner with a tribute video as he emerged from the dugout. The display left him wiping away tears as he entered the visiting dugout.

The Tigers dealt Skubal to the Dodgers on Aug. 2 , in exchange for prospects Zyhir Hope, River Ryan and Brady Smith. The move created a potential super-rotation for the Dodgers, while the Tigers all but admitted they either weren't contending this season or didn't expect to sign Skubal when he hits free agency later this year.

After wiping away tears, Skubal took the mound and did what he usually did there before the trade. It was a strong start in a vacuum: 6 innings, 4 hits, 1 run, 0 walks and 7 strikeouts in a 2-1 Dodgers win.

The start began with a leadoff double from Gleyber Torres, but Skubal recovered with two straight strikeouts then a flyout from Dillon Dingler. He retired 12 straight batters after that double, but allowed his lone run after a leadoff double from Eduardo Valencia and RBI triple from Max Clark.

Skubal exited with the game tied 1-1 and at only 83 pitches, replaced by reliever Evan Phillips. It was a conspicuously quick hook — he had thrown more pitches in every one of his other Dodgers starts — but the team might have been hesitant to push him too much on what was already an emotional day.

The decision did not come back to bite them. The Dodgers bullpen proceeded to allow only one hit across three shutout innings, while Freddie Freeman brought in the winning run with a single in the eighth inning.

The Dodgers are now 3-2 in Skubal's starts.

articles.title: Chris Sale turns back clock, hits triple digits and completes gem on emotional night in Braves sweep
articles.summary: Drake Baldwin's first-pitch homer off Yoshinobu Yamamoto was all Chris Sale needed to shut out the Dodgers with 11 strikeouts and zero walks.
articles.body: Chris Sale, the 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner, had thrown 97 pitches through eight innings Thursday when he walked the length of the Atlanta Braves’ dugout, found manager Walt Weiss and made his intentions clear. "This is mine," Sale declared. The left-hander needed just 12 more pitches to record the final three outs and complete a 1-0 shutout of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in Atlanta. The victory capped a three-game sweep for the NL East-leading Braves, who beat Los Angeles by one run in each game. At 37, Sale’s standout performance Thursday offered another reminder that he remains among baseball’s best and reinforced his standing in the NL Cy Young Award race alongside Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski. BREWERS HUMAN HOWITZER JACOB MISIOROWSKI BREAKS HIS OWN RECORD FOR HARDEST PITCH THROWN BY A STARTER Sale unleashed two of his fastest pitches since 2018 on Thursday, with both being hurled while Shohei Ohtani stood in the batter's box. Sale also record his first complete game since 2019. His ERA now sits at 2.06, which is second in the majors only behind Misiorowski. The Braves ace also extended his streak of starts allowing three runs or fewer to 21. Ohtani struck out twice against Sale, who finished the night with 11 strikeouts. "You can make an argument that, as great a career as he's having, he's as good now as he's ever been," Weiss said. "It's mind-boggling." The last time Sale’s fastball reached triple digits was July 6, 2018, when he was 29 and still pitching for the Boston Red Sox. Boston went on to win the World Series that season, years before Sale would need to undergo Tommy John surgery. "Anytime you're facing a team like that you just try to put your best foot forward, you know it's going to be a dog fight, you know it's not going to come easy," Sale told "The Pat McAfee Show" on Friday. Only one Dodgers player managed to reach scoring position while Sale was on the mound. Videos shared on social media showed Sale’s son reacting as he realized his father would return to the mound for the ninth inning. "The family stuff, it's fun just [because], I'm glad I don't see that stuff until after the game [beacuse] that's just so special," Sale told "The Pat McAfee Show" about the emotional night. DODGERS' TARIK SKUBAL EXPECTS AN EMOTIONAL REUNION AGAINST TIGERS FRIDAY Adding to the emotion of the night, Sale took the mound carrying the weight of a personal loss. Before the game, he learned that Ashley Foss, a close family friend, had died of cancer. Foss’ family has managed Sale’s finances through their agency for several years, and the families have grown close over time. While Sale’s performance took center stage, Yoshinobu Yamamoto was strong for the Dodgers as well. The reigning World Series MVP pitched 6.1 innings, allowing one run on Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s first-pitch solo homer off a splitter. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Braves remain home this weekend, opening a three-game series against the Colorado Rockies on Friday night. The Dodgers, meanwhile, traveled to Detroit for a matchup with the Tigers, with Tarik Skubal facing his former team for the first time since his blockbuster trade to Los Angeles earlier this month.

articles.title: Henderson allows 1 hit in 7 innings as the MLB-leading Brewers beat the Rangers 6-1
articles.summary: Logan Henderson gave up one hit over seven innings and Jake Bauers reached base five times and scored twice in his return to the lineup as the Milwaukee Brew...
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Logan Henderson gave up one hit over seven innings and Jake Bauers reached base five times and scored twice in his return to the lineup as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Texas Rangers 6-1 on Friday night.

Henderson (9-2), who has allowed three runs or less in each of his first 19 career starts, including 14 this season, gave up one run, struck out seven and didn't walk a batter in matching the longest outing of his career, on Aug. 16 against the Dodgers in Los Angeles.

Bauers, who missed three consecutive games with shin splints, went 2 for 2 with three walks, two runs scored and a stolen base.

The Brewers (84-51), who have the best record in the majors, moved a season-high eight games ahead of the Chicago Cubs for the top spot in the NL Central. Texas has lost 13 of its last 16 games on the road.

The Brewers jumped on Rangers starter Cody Bradford (0-3) in the first. Brice Turang had a bunt single and took second on a throwing error. Turang tagged on Jackson Chourio's fly out and scored on William Contreras' groundout. Christian Yelich's run-scoring double gave Milwaukee a 2-0 lead.

Danny Jansen's solo home run off Henderson cut the lead to 2-1 in third.

The Brewers regained a two-run lead in the sixth on David Hamilton's RBI single that chased Bradford, who gave up nine hits and three runs in 5 2/3 innings.

In the seventh, Bauers walked, stole second and scored on Contreras' single to extend the lead to 4-1.

Milwaukee opened the eighth with consecutive bunt singles by Sal Frelick and Hamilton and tacked on two more runs on Jackson Chourio's single and a Contreras sacrifice fly.

Rangers RHP Cal Quantrill (6-4, 2.90 ERA) is scheduled to face Brewers LHP Shane Drohan (6-5, 3.84) on Saturday.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal Reacts to Detroit Return to Face Tigers After Dodgers Trade at MLB Deadline
articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal says he feels he managed to control his emotions while starting against the Detroit Tigers for the first time in his MLB career.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal says he feels he managed to control his emotions while starting against the Detroit Tigers for the first time in his MLB career.

Skubal struck out seven batters and allowed one run in a six-inning no decision as the Dodgers claimed a 2-1 Friday night win at Comerica Park.

"I think I did a good job of keeping baseball, baseball," Skubal said after the Dodgers' win. "And trying to compete, and give our team a chance to win.

"I think you kind of saw the emotions early, but I feel like I did a good job keeping the game baseball. But obviously, this place is special to me."

Skubal played the first six and a half seasons of his MLB career with Detroit.

He was traded to the Dodgers earlier this month after failing to work out an extension with the Tigers, although he has since indicated he has not ruled out a return to Detroit in the future.

The two-time reigning AL Cy Young Award winner told reporters he had an emotional reaction in the tunnel after watching a tribute video the Tigers played for him ahead of Friday's start.

"It's tough. This is a place I've known my entire career, since 2018," Skubal said. "It was special, for sure."

He added that fans were "pretty supportive" and that he planned to assume any potential boos from the crowd were people cheering "Skub."

Skubal was pulled from the game after six innings, 83 pitches and a long dugout conversation with manager Dave Roberts.

The pitcher said afterward he felt "still in control of the baseball game" when he was pulled.

"Of course I did want to go back out there. Some of those decisions aren't my decisions," Skubal said. "Doc kind of came to me and said we've got a long road. He said he's kind of pushed me, recently."

Skubal threw more than 100 pitches in each of his last two starts prior to Friday's outing. Roberts will be tasked with not overworking the Dodgers' newest ace before his club begins a bid to three-peat as World Series champions this fall.
